chunks: From him, from Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, who said:

I asked Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and said: 'May I be your ransom, indeed the people of Al-Jabal find the marks of sheep heavy [to remove], so they cut their marks.' He said: 'They are forbidden.' I said: 'May I be your ransom, do we seek good omen [by cutting them]?' He said: 'Do you not know that it touches the hand and the garment, and it is forbidden?'

key_terms.أَيَاتُ الْغَنَمِ: The marks or signs on sheep, often used for divination
key_terms.تَثْقُلُ: They find it heavy or burdensome
key_terms.فَنَسْتَصْبِحُ بِهَا: We seek good omens through them

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on cutting sheep marks for fortune-telling in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam Al-Reza (peace be upon him) clarifies the ruling on 'cutting the marks' (ayāt) of sheep, a pre-Islamic practice used for divination or seeking omens. He declares the practice forbidden (ḥarām) not only due to its association with superstition but also because the physical act of cutting renders the hand and garment ritually impure (najis) or requiring purification, thereby linking ritual purity with the rejection of pagan customs.
